passages.quote:
National journeys within the UK and between the UK and EU are governed by the assimilated (EU retained) drivers’ hours and tachograph rules.

AETR rules apply to international journeys that are not wholly between the UK and EU and are to or through a country that is a signatory to the AETR agreement, including journeys involving Norway and Switzerland.

Introduction

The aim of this guidance is to provide industry with detailed information on the drivers’ hours and working time rules and how to deal with emergency and urgent situations, particularly when and how to request a temporary relaxation of the drivers’ hours rules.

It is important to remember that these rules are in place to protect road safety and the working conditions of drivers and to reduce the risk of drivers being involved in fatigue-related accidents. Therefore, any relaxation of the rules must be a last resort.

Industry must continue to put contingency plans in place to deal with emergency and urgent situations – particularly to deal with adverse weather conditions, which can normally be expected during the winter period.

Background

Following the UK’s departure from the European Union (EU), national journeys within the UK and between the UK and EU are governed by the assimilated drivers’ hours and tachograph rules (Regulation (EC) 561/2006[footnote 1] and Regulation (EU) 165/2014[footnote 2], as they have effect in the UK). The sector-specific Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations 2005[footnote 3] limit the amount of driving and working time that can be carried out by most heavy goods vehicle (HGV) drivers, and around 30% of bus and coach drivers in the UK.

The Great Britain (GB) domestic drivers’ hours rules (Part VI of the Transport Act 1968, as amended) apply to most goods and passenger vehicles that are exempt from the assimilated drivers’ hours rules. Further details on these rules can be found in Annex A of this guidance.

The assimilated drivers’ hours rules do not apply to vehicles used in emergencies or rescue operations. In addition to this, the rules also allow relaxations to be made administratively in urgent circumstances for up to 30 days. Any relaxation of the assimilated drivers’ hours rules for longer than 30 days, in exceptional circumstances, requires the prior authorisation of the Secretary of State for Transport and needs to be implemented via regulations.

Before we left the EU, for longer relaxations we needed the prior authorisation of the European Commission.

Any relaxation of the GB domestic drivers’ hours rules is the responsibility of the Department for Transport (DfT). A summary of the legislation that provides the powers to relax the rules can be found in Annex B of this guidance.

The assimilated drivers’ hours and sector-specific working time rules are applicable in Northern Ireland (NI), although the NI government is responsible for implementation, enforcement and handling of any relaxation requests for this region. NI also has its own domestic drivers’ hours rules – the Transport Act 1968 does not apply there and any requests for a relaxation of the domestic rules in NI should also be directed to the Department for Infrastructure at the NI government.

Unforeseen events

Where an infringement of the GB domestic drivers’ hours rules occurs, the law protects from conviction in court those drivers who can prove that the infringement was due to unavoidable delay in the completion of a journey arising out of circumstances that they could not reasonably have foreseen.

In order to deal with unavoidable delays during the course of a journey, a driver may depart from either:

(a) the assimilated or AETR rules to reach a suitable stopping place to ensure the safety of persons, the vehicle or its load

(b) the assimilated rules only to reach their operational base or home in exceptional circumstances

These provisions are for instances where it unexpectedly becomes impossible to comply with the rules on drivers’ hours during the course of a journey.

Planned breaches of the rules are not allowed. This means that when an unforeseen event occurs it would be for the driver to decide whether it is necessary to depart from the rules.

Some examples of such events are delays caused by:

severe weather

road traffic accidents

mechanical breakdowns

interruptions of ferry services

any event that causes or is likely to cause danger to the life or health of people or animals

Reaching a suitable stopping place

Provided that road safety is not jeopardised and to enable the vehicle to reach a suitable stopping place, a driver may depart from the assimilated drivers’ hours rules to the extent necessary to ensure the safety of persons, the vehicle or its load.

Note that this concession only allows for drivers to reach a suitable stopping place, not necessarily to complete their planned journey.

Although a ‘suitable stopping place’ is not defined in the assimilated drivers’ hours rules, the legislation is quite specific about when a driver can deviate from the rules (to ensure safety of persons, vehicles or its load).

Therefore, what a driver is carrying will determine where it would be suitable for them to stop, such as drivers of vehicles carrying:

perishable loads (may need to stop near refrigeration facilities)

high-value loads (may need to stop where they can secure the load)

live animals (may need to stop where care can be provided for animals)

passengers (may need to stop where passengers can rest and have refreshments)

Drivers must note all the reasons for deviating from the rules at the latest on reaching the suitable stopping place:

on the back of their tachograph record sheets – if using an analogue tachograph

on a printout or temporary sheet – if using a digital or smart tachograph

Reaching the employer’s operational centre or driver’s home

Timescales

Once sufficient evidence has been provided and DfT ministers are content that a relaxation is justified under Article 14(2) of the assimilated drivers’ hours rules, the process to make an informal administrative relaxation of enforcement of the rules should take no more than 24 hours[footnote 6].

Where an exemption under Article 3(d) of the assimilated rules is appropriate in all circumstances, DfT’s confirmation of it will still be required in order to ensure that DVSA relaxes enforcement in respect of the drivers affected but such confirmation should normally be provided without delay, particularly where some advance indication has been received.

Annex A: assimilated and domestic drivers’ hours and the road transport working time rules

The assimilated drivers’ hours rules (Regulation (EC) 561/2006 as it has effect in the UK)

The rules apply to goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes and passenger carrying vehicles with 10 or more seats, unless covered by a range of specific UK/EU-wide exemptions and national derogations relating to the type of vehicle and/or its use. See Annex D for a list of the exemptions and national derogations. Drivers in scope of the assimilated rules are required to use a tachograph.

There are many exceptions but the main assimilated driver rules limits are:

9 hours maximum daily driving

56 hours maximum weekly driving

90 hours maximum fortnightly driving

11 hours minimum daily rest

45 hours minimum weekly rest

45-minute breaks for every 4.5 hours driving

GB domestic drivers’ hours rules[footnote 7]

Drivers of vehicles that are outside the scope of the assimilated rules are, with a limited range of exceptions, covered by the GB domestic rules.

The following sectors are likely to work under the domestic rules:

vans not exceeding 3.5 tonnes

tradesmen (for example, building or construction)

passenger transport (operating on regular routes up to 31 miles (50km))

NHS and publicly owned medical vehicles

refuse collection

local authority services for the elderly and disabled

milk (not including bulk milk tankers)

utilities and road maintenance (for example, gas or water)

breakdown

agricultural, fishing and forestry (used within a 62-mile (100km) radius from the base of operations)

charity work (where employed drivers are used)

special vehicles (such as vehicles that operate on natural gas/electric or are not capable of speeds over 24mph (40km/h))

‘gritters’ – vehicles designed for the spreading of rock salt directly onto roads or pavements

The main limits and requirements for goods vehicle drivers are:

10 hours maximum daily driving

11 hours maximum daily duty

The main limits and requirements for passenger vehicle drivers are:

10 hours maximum daily driving

16 hours maximum daily duty

10 hours daily rest

no weekly rest requirement

at least one period of 24 hours off duty in any 2 consecutive weeks

Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations 2005 (SI 2005/639)

These regulations apply to mobile workers (that is drivers and crew) who work on vehicles subject to the assimilated drivers’ hours rules.

The regulations stipulate a maximum 48-hour average week and no more than 60 hours in any single week (there is no opt out). If working at night then mobile workers must not work over 10 hours in any 24-hour period, unless a collective or workforce agreement is in place (night-time is the period between midnight and 4:00am for goods vehicles and between 1:00am and 5:00am for passenger vehicles).

The regulations also provide minimum levels of breaks as follows:

30 minutes if daily working totals 6 to 9 hours

45 minutes of breaks (one of which must be at least 15 minutes long) if working over 9 hours

the same rest requirements as the assimilated rules

Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833)

These regulations apply to mobile workers (drivers and crew) who work on vehicles subject to the domestic drivers’ hours rules.

As mobile workers, only certain requirements apply, namely:

average weekly working time of 48 hours (with the possibility to opt out)

health checks for night workers

requirement for ‘adequate rest’[footnote 8] (the length of which is not defined)

Workers not in-scope of either the domestic or assimilated drivers’ hours rules need to comply with all the rules of the Working Time Regulations 1998, as amended, these include the right to:

1 uninterrupted 20-minute rest break during their working day (this could be a tea or lunch break), if they work more than 6 hours a day

11 hours rest between working days

an uninterrupted 24 hours without any work each week

48 hours each fortnight

Annex B: Relevant legislation

International transport

The assimilated drivers’ hours rules do not apply to ‘vehicles used in emergencies or rescue operations’ (Article 3(d) Regulation (EC) 561/2006). These rules do not define an ‘emergency’ but DfT considers this would include any of the situations that would be considered an emergency for the purposes of the GB domestic drivers’ hours legislation.

Article 14(2) of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 – as it has effect in the UK – also provides the Secretary of State for Transport with the power to grant an administrative temporary relaxation of drivers’ hours rules for a period that does not exceed 30 days in an urgent case.
